The Priesthood Executive Council directed the Curriculum Department and church auxiliaries, including Primary, Young Men, Young Women, Relief Society, and Sunday School. This council was composed of members of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, the Quorums of the Seventy, and the Presiding Bishopric. Auxiliary presidencies attended frequently to report and discuss issues related to their spheres of responsibility. (Lee Tom Perry, Paul M. Bons, and Alan L. Wilkins, “Contemporary Organization,” inEncyclopedia of Mormonism,ed. Daniel H. Ludlow, 5 vols. [New York: Macmillan, 1992], 3:1046.)

During the early 1990s, chapels throughout the Philippines had sewing machines to help Relief Society members learn to sew. Many members used these skills to earn money for their families. (See Marvin K. Gardner,“Philippine Saints: A Believing People,”Ensign21, no. 7 [July 1991]: 37.)

Road shows were short musical programs that local Mutual Improvement Association (MIA) groups wrote and performed in their wards and stakes. These began by the 1920s. Laurel is the name given to the group of young women aged sixteen to eighteen years. (“M. I. A. Notes: Stake Happenings,”Young Woman’s Journal34, no. 7 [July 1923]: 393; Elaine Anderson Cannon, “Young Women,” in Ludlow,Encyclopedia of Mormonism,4:1617–1618.)

The Relief Society general board adopted the motto “Charity Never Faileth,” from1 Corinthians 13:8, in 1913. (Jill Mulvay Derr, Janath Russell Cannon, and Maureen Ursenbach Beecher,Women of Covenant: The Story of Relief Society[Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1992], 194.)

Clyde taught English at Brigham Young University for ten years, then worked as a certified construction flagger, helping other flaggers keep their jobs when they had to miss work for a personal or family illness. She chaired the Utah Task Force on Gender and Justice from 1987 to 1990 and was citizen chair of the Utah Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice until 1988, when she began twelve years of service on the Utah State Board of Regents. (Aileen Clyde, emails to Kate Holbrook, July 21, 2015, and Jan. 20, 2016; Aileen H. Clyde 20th Century Women’s Legacy Archive, accessed Dec. 8, 2015,lib.utah.edu.)

Before updating the purpose statement, Jack and her counselors reviewed earlier statements—paying particular attention to the purpose as recorded in the Nauvoo Relief Society minutes and to statements written by previous presidencies—and then developed their own, which emphasized action and the individual woman. They wanted to create a statement that would be meaningful for women around the world. (Cherry B. Silver,History of the Relief Society: The Elaine Jack Administration[Salt Lake City: Relief Society of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, 2000], 5–6, CHL; Jill Mulvay Derr, Janath Russell Cannon, and Maureen Ursenbach Beecher,Women of Covenant: The Story of Relief Society[Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1992], 401–403.)
